newsitem.title: UK: Britain's car industry breathes easy after budget.
newsitem.headline: Britain's car industry breathes easy after budget.

text.p: Britain's car industry breathed a sigh of relief after today's budget, industry leaders said on Wednesday.
The industry had been bracing itself for an attack on all fronts, with the Labour party's first budget in nearly 20 years.

The industry was seen by many commentators as an easy target for extra revenue raising, with the added temptation that many measures designed to soak the motorist could have be been dressed up as caring measures to protect the environment.

Instead of an all-out attack, Chancellor Gordon Brown announced an increase of an extra one per cent a year in fuel duty above the annual five per cent increase established by the previous government.
Brown also cut the tax by 500 pounds a year on trucks and buses that meet low, unspecified, emission standards.
"We feel extremely favourable about the budget. We were waiting to get a bit of a hiding," said Neil Reeve, spokesman for the Retail Motor Industry Federation.

The industry had feared a range of tax changes, including a graded annual tax which would have cost more for big cars, changes to company car taxation, and much bigger increases in petrol and diesel prices.
"This seems quite constructive, there are many good points," said Roger King, director of public affairs at the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.
"There is some relief that the Chancellor hasn't graded excise duty on bigger cars. That would have created problems for manufacturers in the U.K. These cars are mainly for export," said King.

"We are pleased that the Chancellor hasn't decided to introduce draconian measures on the company car. But (Chief Secretary to the Treasury Alistair) Darling is looking at various ways of tackling tax evasion and we suspect a review of the company car tax regime will be in there," King said.
King said the SMMT welcomed the concession for a lower licence fee on trucks and buses which cut pollution.
"But 500 pounds is really too low for them (operators) to trade in old smokers. We need to go a little bit further for this to impact the market," King said.
King said he was disappointed that some of the extra two billion a year raised from petrol tax was not ring-fenced for envrionmental projects like public transport.
The Chief executive of the Retail Motor Federation, Christopher Macgowan, said the budget showed the government had listened to arguments put forward by the industry.
"The car industry is too big and important to be meddled with. Our arguments have been listened too, and that's good news," Macgowan said.
